p.title: Large Language Model Enhanced Logic Tensor Network for Stance Detection

ext.title: Large Language Model Enhanced Logic Tensor Network for Stance Detection
ext.year: 2025 (volume year; published online 29 Nov 2024; received 25 May 2024, accepted 22 Nov 2024)
ext.document_type: Journal article (Full Length Article), machine learning / NLP
ext.coverage: Read the full text file in two chunks (lines 1-1168 and 1169-1390 of 1390), covering front matter, abstract, introduction, related work, methodology (Sections 3.1-3.3, Eqs 1-14), experiments (Sections 4.1-4.9, Tables 1-6), conclusion, CRediT/data statement, and the full reference list. Figures 1-5 (framework, CoT illustration, toy FOL, ablation bar chart, GPT-4 vs GPT-3.5 chart) are not present as text, so their values are not reported. Table column alignment in the text extraction is partly ambiguous; values are reported in the header order given in the text. No Paul markup file was supplied (the markup list was "(none)"), so paul_markup is empty. Metadata hint was correct on title, authors and venue; corrected to add the volume/article number, online date and DOI.
ext.research_question: Can first-order logic (FOL) rules elicited from LLMs by chain-of-thought prompting be encoded in a logic tensor network (LTN), and can fusing LTNs built from several LLMs produce interpretable and more accurate stance detection than fine-tuned PLMs, prompt-tuning, and LLM-only baselines, in both in-target and zero-shot settings?
ext.theory: Neurosymbolic learning: logic tensor networks (real logic with soft/product-style operators, after Badreddine et al. 2022) make predicates differentiable so that FOL rules constrain a deep network trained by backpropagation. Motivation draws on FOL-distillation work (Hu et al. 2016 DNNLR; posterior regularization) and on chain-of-thought prompting of LLMs. The paper asserts interpretability through FOL rationales; there is no formal interpretability test.
ext.data: Three English-language stance benchmarks. (1) SemEval-2016 Task 6 (SEM16; Mohammad et al. 2016): targets FM, LA, HC, DT (plus Ath and CC are named); Table 1 counts favor/against/neutral: DT 148/299/260 (707 total), HC 163/565/256 (984), LA 167/544/222 (933), FM 268/511/170 (949), so about 3,573 instances across the four targets listed. 15 percent of training data held out as dev. Unit: sentence-target pair (tweet). (2) VAST (Allaway and McKeown 2020): Table 2 lists 13,477 train / 2,062 dev / 3,006 test examples with stance labels Pro/Con/Neutral; the row labels for topic counts appear misaligned in the extraction (for example "#Zero-shot Topics 4003"). Evaluated on zero-shot topics under 100 percent and 10 percent training data. (3) ISD (Huang et al. 2023): text says 6,027 labeled tweets about DT_I and JB_I, averaging 2.14 hashtags per sentence, 80/20 train/test split; however Table 1 ISD rows sum to 5,588 (DT_I 3,105; JB_I 2,483), a discrepancy. Time period of data collection: not stated in the text. Population: social media posts about political figures and topics (abortion, feminism, Clinton, Trump, Biden, bike lanes, rail, cameras). LLM outputs come from gpt-3.5-turbo-0301, Claude-2-100k and LLaMA-2-70b-chat (temperature 0); GPT-4 appears only in Figure 5 (not extracted).
ext.method: FOLAR = three modules. (a) Knowledge Elicitation (Sec 3.1): chain-of-thought prompts ask an LLM to produce a FOL rule for each input and target, illustrated by Eq 1 and Table 5. (b) LTN (Sec 3.2): predicates are phrases embedded by a shared pretrained BERT, followed by fully connected layers; soft-logic operators are negation 1-U, conjunction product, disjunction U1+U2-U1U2, implication 1-U1+U1U2 (Eqs 2-5); output is a softmax over favor/neutral/against (Eq 6 composition). (c) Multi-Decision Fusion (Sec 3.3): one LTN per LLM (GPT-3.5, LLaMA-2, Claude-2), representation vectors concatenated into H and fused by attention-based dynamic routing over t iterations with layer normalization and sigmoid (Eqs 7-11); training minimizes cross-entropy (Eq 12). Training: AdamW, batch 16, up to 30 epochs, warm-up ratio 0.2, learning rate 1e-5, weight decay 1e-3. Baselines (Sec 4.4): statistical (Bicond, CrossNet, SEKT, TPDG); PLM (JoinCL, PT-HCL, TarBK, SDAgu, KPT, KEprompt, BERT-FT); LLM (Ts-CoT, KASD, MPPT, COLA) plus FOL-CoT (the LLM-only variant of FOLAR). Ablations: w/o FOL (compared to Ts-CoT-like structure), w/o LTN, w/o MDF (single GPT-3.5).
ext.identification: None in the causal sense. This is a predictive supervised classification benchmark. Generalization is tested by holding out targets (zero-shot: train on other SEM16 targets, test on one held-out target; VAST zero-shot topics) and by a 10 percent training-data condition on VAST. Each result is the average of three runs.
ext.scope: Population: English social media posts (tweets and similar short texts) with stance toward a named target, mostly US political figures and contentious topics. Institution: Shenzhen Technology University and collaborators (no institutional sample). Era: SEM16 (2016) and VAST (2020) benchmarks; LLM snapshots from 2023 (GPT-3.5-turbo-0301, Claude-2, LLaMA-2-70b). Not about lobbying, legislators, campaigns, networks, path-finding, allocation, elections as events, persuasion or turnout. Relevant to the project only as a text-measurement method (stance labeling of political text) and as an interpretable neurosymbolic classifier.

key_findings.finding: In-target SEM16 and ISD (Table 3, F_avg, three runs): FOLAR scores FM 70.6, LA 72.7*, HC 84.5*, DT_I 73.3*, JB_I 71.5*. The text says FOLAR beats the strongest competitor by 1.7 points on LA (COLA 71.0 per the table) and 2.0 points on DT_I (MPPT 71.3). FOLAR is not the top row on every column: FOL-CoT/w-o-MDF variant reports HC 85.5 and KEprompt reports FM 72.1 in the extracted table.
key_findings.numbers: FOLAR LA 72.7 vs COLA 71.0 (+1.7); DT_I 73.3 vs MPPT 71.3 (+2.0); HC 84.5 vs w/o MDF 85.5; FM 70.6 vs KEprompt 72.1. Text: BERT-FT beats TPDG by 5.3 percent on ISD; KEprompt beats BERT-FT by 6.7 on LA.

key_findings.finding: Zero-shot SEM16 (Table 4, F_avg): FOLAR scores HC 85.3*, FM 73.7*, LA 71.9*, DT 70.9 (not marked significant). Best SEM16 competitors in the table are Ts-CoT HC 83.2 and MPPT FM 70.9, LA 70.1.
key_findings.numbers: FOLAR HC 85.3 vs Ts-CoT 83.2; FM 73.7 vs MPPT 70.9; LA 71.9 vs MPPT 70.1; DT 70.9 vs MPPT 70.7.

key_findings.finding: Zero-shot VAST: FOLAR gains are larger in the 10 percent-data condition. Text reports +4.2 points on VAST (100 percent) and +6.2 points on VAST (10 percent) over the best competitor, consistent with All-column values FOLAR 81.0 vs KASD 76.8 and FOLAR 80.2 vs MPPT 74.0.

Ablation, multi-decision fusion: removing MDF (single GPT-3.5 LTN) lowers zero-shot VAST scores. Derived gaps from Table 4 are about 5.8 points (100 percent) and 5.3 points (10 percent). The text says the drop is significant but does not give test statistics.
key_findings.numbers: wo/MDF All: 75.2 (VAST 100%) and 74.9 (VAST 10%) vs full FOLAR 81.0 and 80.2. SEM16 zero-shot wo/MDF: HC 74.1, FM 71.8, LA 71.2, DT 69.7 vs FOLAR 85.3, 73.7, 71.9, 70.9. Fig 4 values not extractable.

key_findings.finding: LLM-only chain-of-thought with FOL rationales (FOL-CoT, no LTN training) beats Ts-CoT on VAST zero-shot. The FOL-CoT All values are identical in both VAST rows (79.8), which may be a copy error in the table.
key_findings.numbers: FOL-CoT VAST(100%) All 79.8 vs Ts-CoT 73.4; FOL-CoT VAST(10%) All 79.8 vs Ts-CoT 70.3; FOL-CoT SEM16 HC 83.6 vs Ts-CoT 83.2.

key_findings.finding: Manual check of FOL quality: three NLP researchers with master's degrees rated 100 randomly sampled test explanations on salience, non-redundancy and non-contradiction. Agreement (kappa, type not specified) exceeded 70 percent on all three criteria, averaging 76 percent.
key_findings.numbers: n = 100 instances; 3 raters; kappa > 0.70 per criterion; mean 0.76.

key_findings.finding: Error analysis of 50 incorrect VAST predictions: two failure types, (a) implicit or sarcastic stance that the KE step cannot capture (for example the phrase 'master race'), and (b) over-inference by the LLM when clauses carry opposing polarity or the LLM links unrelated positive words to the target.

Case study (Table 5): three examples where FOLAR's FOL rationales produce the correct label (bike lane - Against; camera - Support; Hillary Clinton - Against) while the baseline fails. Qualitative only; no counts given.

measures: Average F1 of favor and against, F_avg (Eq 13), for SEM16 and ISD
Average F of favor, against and neutral, F_avg (Eq 14), for VAST
Statistical significance marked at p < 0.05 (test not named)
Kappa agreement (type not stated) for manual FOL quality ratings, three criteria
Accuracy-style claims in text are F-score based; no accuracy table
limitations: The paper has no dedicated limitations section. Authors list future work: more complex logic forms, more contentious topics, newer dynamic logic, and better decision fusion (Conclusion, lines 1199-1206).
Implicit or sarcastic stance is not captured by LLM-elicited FOL (Sec 4.8, lines 1149-1157).
LLM over-inference and clause-level polarity conflicts cause errors (Sec 4.8, lines 1158-1167).
Results come from three runs with no reported standard deviations or confidence intervals; significance test (p < 0.05) is not named (lines 703-711).
Relies on proprietary, versioned LLM APIs (gpt-3.5-turbo-0301, Claude-2-100k) and temperature 0 to aid reproducibility; GPT-4 results appear only in a figure (lines 532-543, 1019-1025).
Data availability is stated as 'available on request' (line 1224), while the abstract says source code will be publicly available (lines 29-30).
Inconsistent SEM16 target handling: DT, Ath and CC are said to be excluded (lines 503-504) but DT is used in the zero-shot tables and the setting list (lines 509, 739).
ISD size: text says 6,027 tweets (line 515) but Table 1 rows sum to 5,588 (lines 463-471).
Table 2 topic-count rows look misaligned (for example '#Zero-shot Topics 4003' larger than examples per split logic) (lines 485-492).
FOL-CoT All values are identical in both VAST rows of Table 4 (79.8), suggesting a transcription or copy error (lines 903-913).
Fusion ablation (w/o MDF) uses only one LLM (GPT-3.5), so it does not separate MDF from simply choosing a different LLM (lines 1004-1009).
Manual FOL check uses only 100 instances and three raters, and the kappa variant is not specified (lines 1181-1185).
Gains over baselines are small on several in-target columns (for example FM, where KEprompt is higher in the extracted table).
references_of_note: Badreddine, d'Avila Garcez, Serafini & Spranger (2022), Logic tensor networks, Artificial Intelligence 303: the LTN formalism the paper builds on (core neurosymbolic reference).
Bianchi & Hitzler (2019), On the capabilities of logic tensor networks for deductive reasoning (AAAI spring symposium): LTN soft-logic use for ontological reasoning.
Hu, Ma, Liu, Hovy & Xing (2016), Harnessing deep neural networks with logic rules (ACL): DNNLR, FOL knowledge distilled into networks via posterior regularization.
Hu, Yang, Salakhutdinov & Xing (2016), Deep neural networks with massive learned knowledge (EMNLP): extension of logic-rule integration.
Zhang, Huang et al. (2022), Sentiment interpretable logic tensor network for aspect-term sentiment analysis (COLING): the authors' prior SILTN work with manually crafted FOL.
Huang, Zhang et al. (2022), Logic tensor network with massive learned knowledge for aspect-based sentiment analysis (Knowledge-Based Systems 257): LTN grounding via fully connected layers.
Huang et al. (2023), Knowledge-enhanced prompt-tuning for stance detection (TALLIP 22(6)): source of the ISD dataset and KEprompt baseline.
Mohammad et al. (2016), SemEval-2016 Task 6: Detecting stance in tweets: source of SEM16 with political targets (Hillary Clinton, Donald Trump).
Allaway & McKeown (2020), Zero-shot stance detection: a dataset and model using generalized topic representations (EMNLP): VAST corpus.

Zhang, Ding & Jing (2022), How would stance detection techniques evolve after the launch of ChatGPT?; Zhang, Fu, Ding et al. (2023), Investigating chain-of-thought with ChatGPT for stance detection (Ts-CoT).

Li, Liang et al. (2023), Stance detection on social media with background knowledge (KASD); Ding et al. (2024), cross-target stance detection via target analytical perspectives (MPPT); Lan et al. (2023), collaborative role-infused LLM agents (COLA): the LLM-based stance baselines.
Liang et al. (2021/2022), TPDG, PT-HCL, JointCL: cross-target contrastive and graph baselines on the same benchmarks.
Wei and Chain-of-thought lineage: Ling et al. (2023), Deductive verification of chain-of-thought reasoning (cited for CoT verification).

short_quotes.quote: The FOL aids in organizing reasoning and visualizing decisions for stance detection
LLMs often exhibit bias in knowledge elicitation due to variations in their self-learning from training datasets and methodologies.
This alignment with first-order logic ensures that the model's decisions are both interpretable and data-driven.

rel.summary_md:
Dai et al. (Neural Networks 183, 2025) propose FOLAR, a stance detector with three parts. First, chain-of-thought prompts ask an LLM to write a first-order-logic (FOL) rule for each text and target. Second, a logic tensor network (LTN) uses a shared BERT and soft operators (negation 1-U, product conjunction, implication 1-U1+U1U2) to turn the rule into a differentiable classifier. Third, the LTNs built from GPT-3.5, Claude-2 and LLaMA-2 are fused by attention routing. The tests use English political tweets (SemEval-2016, ISD) and VAST. On in-target SEM16 and ISD the gains are small: +1.7 F_avg on LA and +2.0 on DT_I, and FOLAR is not the best on FM or HC. Zero-shot VAST gains are larger: +4.2 with full training data and +6.2 with 10% of it. The fusion ablation is about 5.8 points, but it compares fusion with a single GPT-3.5 model, so fusion is not separated from the choice of LLM. The paper reports no standard deviations, does not name its significance test, and its tables contain internal inconsistencies. The interpretability claim rests only on a 100-item, 3-rater check.

For Paul's system, the paper matters most as a formal version of something already built. The two-hop CU-alignment rule in fec/stance/apply_two_hop_stance.py composes stance with valence by hard sign multiplication over a hand-curated registry. FOLAR is the soft, learned, LLM-elicited form of that rule. It also gives a candidate route for the registry-coverage problem, but its error analysis (the LLM linking unrelated positive words to the target) names the same failure that sank the system's automatic-registry variants. The fusion result points to a cheap check on single-labeller bias in the Claude pre-labels that the DEBATE reader distils. It does not show that switching to FOLAR would beat a fine-tuned DEBATE or SVM on 87 to 156 held-out CU press items. The domain, the text genre and the LLM versions all differ.

bearings.paper_claim: FOL rules elicited from an LLM (for example, a target linked to a negative consequence implies Against) are made differentiable with product-logic operators (conjunction U1*U2, implication 1-U1+U1U2) and trained end to end. The paper reports this improves zero-shot VAST F_avg to 81.0, against 76.8 for the best baseline. The error analysis of 50 VAST errors names LLM over-inference that links unrelated positive words to the target, and clause-level polarity conflicts.
bearings.system_side: compose() is a hard Boolean version of the same rule: stance(speaker to target) and valence(target to CU) give alignment by sign flip. Valence is looked up by substring match in a curated registry, and the flat model alignment is the fallback on a registry miss. Reported results: stance hop 0.915, valence hop 0.689, registry composition 0.782 / F1 0.754 against a flat baseline of 0.677. Every automatic-registry variant fell below the flat baseline.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Transfer is limited to the decomposition idea. FOLAR's targets are the benchmark's named targets, whereas the system's valence hop needs CU-specific domain knowledge, which is not in general LLM priors and is owner-judged. The paper's over-inference failure is the system's automatic-registry failure. LLM-elicited valence rules would therefore stay UNVERIFIED (DE-062) until scored against Paul's 400 tweet golds under single-look rules. The soft operators could replace the hard sign rule, but the paper gives no evidence that a soft version beats an exact registry lookup where the registry has coverage.

bearings.paper_claim: Fusing decisions from three LLMs (GPT-3.5, Claude-2, LLaMA-2) beats the single-GPT-3.5 variant by about 5.8 F_avg on zero-shot VAST with 100% of training data (81.0 vs 75.2) and about 5.3 with 10% (80.2 vs 74.9). The authors say LLMs 'exhibit bias in knowledge elicitation' that differs by model.
bearings.paper_location: Sec 3.3, Eqs 7-11; Table 4 wo/MDF row; Sec 4.6; Introduction
bearings.system_side: DEBATE is fine-tuned on 552 labels that a single Claude rater pre-labelled (claude_stance.py, default claude-sonnet-4-6, with a 15-word reason field) and humans overrode. Its stated agreement with Claude is 87.2%. Inference uses the NLI hypothesis template 'This text is {}.'
bearings.transfer_conditions: This bears on the open question of how much DEBATE accuracy is agreement with the LLM pre-labeller rather than with humans. A second and third LLM rater would expose labeller-specific bias before human override. The evidence is weak. The ablation confounds fusion with the choice of LLM, the paper gives no variance, the data are tweets on 2016-2020 benchmark targets rather than CU press releases, and the 2023 model snapshots it used are retired. The paper does not test whether fusion beats a supervised fine-tuned NLI reader on the system's member-grouped held-out sets.

bearings.paper_claim: FOLAR's advantage over its baselines is small in-target (+1.7 LA, +2.0 DT_I; it loses on FM to KEprompt, 72.1 vs 70.6) and larger in low-data zero-shot (+6.2 on VAST with 10% of training data, against +4.2 with 100%). The baselines are PLM, prompt and LLM methods. No TF-IDF/SVM baseline is reported.
bearings.system_side: The best classical reader is LinearSVC on word plus character TF-IDF, at 83.9% / macro-F1 0.816 on the untouched n=87 test. Supervised tweet stance reached 0.737 CV on 399 golds. The stack is fixed, single-target, and has small label sets.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper cannot settle the SVM-versus-LLM question for this corpus because it has no bag-of-words baseline. Its pattern (small in-target gains, larger low-data or new-target gains) suggests an LLM-rule reader would help most on new or rare CU targets, not on the fixed in-target press categories. The evidence is benchmark-level, comes from three runs, and gives no confidence intervals.

gaps_exposed: The valence hop has no soft or probabilistic form: compose() is hard sign multiplication, so valence confidence and partial registry matches are discarded (apply_two_hop_stance.py:27-33).

The pre-labels come from a single LLM (Claude). No second or third LLM rater exists to measure labeller-specific bias before human override, which bears on the open question of how much DEBATE accuracy is LLM agreement.

Claude's reason field is captured (claude_stance.py:93) but is never checked for quality. The paper at least rates rationales for salience, non-redundancy and non-contradiction (n=100, kappa about 0.76).
No low-data or new-target evaluation condition exists for CU stance. The paper shows that method rankings differ most in that condition.
flags: Nothing here conflicts with the SNA wording rules (D-025, D-021, the rejected cosponsorship and normalization proposals). The paper is pure text classification.

Any LLM-elicited FOL rules or valence links adopted from this method are new agent analysis and stay UNVERIFIED until a second path (human gold) reproduces them (DE-062). The paper's own error analysis shows LLM over-inference on target links, the same failure that made the automatic-registry variants fall below the flat baseline.

The paper's quality is weak for adoption. It reports no SDs or CIs over three runs and does not name its significance test. FOL-CoT shows the same 79.8 in both VAST rows (a likely copy error). The ISD counts disagree (6,027 in the text vs 5,588 in the table), and the SEM16 target exclusions are inconsistent. Data are 'available on request', and the gpt-3.5-turbo-0301 and Claude-2 snapshots are retired, so the results cannot be reproduced.
The interpretability claim is asserted, not tested. Do not quote FOLAR rationales as explanations of stance without a separate validation.
rel.paul_alignment: The paper agrees with Paul's endorsement of LLM-based position extraction (Kim J. 2025, Birkenmaier). It also confirms the weakness he flagged, disentangling ambiguous statements: implicit or sarcastic stance and clause-level polarity conflicts are FOLAR's two named failure types. On the two-hop component, the paper's FOL implication operator is a formal answer to his question of how agreement is quantified when actors relate through a third party. The system already answers that question with the stance-times-valence registry, which his notes do not yet record. His notes are stale on that point, not this paper's. Paul has no annotation of Dai et al. The paper does not support replacing the SVM or DEBATE readers, which goes further than his view that bag-of-words baselines are outdated: FOLAR's in-target gains are small, and no SVM baseline was run.

related.why: Same task (stance in political tweets), comparing fine-tuned RoBERTa against traditional ML. It supplies the SVM and PLM comparison that Dai et al. omit.
A direction-aware lexicon addresses clause-level polarity direction, which is one of FOLAR's two error types. The system rejected a whole-text version of that lexicon in bill-sign handling.
General guidance on using LLMs to label political text. It bears on validating FOLAR-style LLM-elicited labels and rationales.
Neural-network stance work from the same journal. Zhou models stance over time, while Dai classifies static stance.
Both use LLMs to extract positions toward a named target. Kim validates against human labels (96.9%), which Dai does not do for stance labels.
